https://www.telegraph.co.uk/opinion/2024.title: A cashless society will struggle to cope with hostile or accidental events
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/opinion/2024.subtitle: Plus: The next Tory leader; Biden out; the rights of disabled commuters; housebuilding pledges; protesters’ arrest; and a better cuppa
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/opinion/2024.text:
SIR – In response to the recent IT failure, which stopped card and digital payment systems from working (report, July 20), an expert interviewed by the BBC recommended we all carry cash just in case. That advice was inadequate. The more normal cashless payments become, the more the facility to handle cash disappears. If we want resilience to cope with malicious and accidental events, then we are all responsible for promoting that. Every time we use cash we are, individually, doing our bit to protect ourselves and society.Peter GrayBelfast
SIR – It was good that I had some cash on me on Friday when trying to check out at the supermarket as all the systems had crashed.I think I was the only one who could pay cash, leaving lots of shoppers looking totally bewildered.J KibbleWoking, Surrey
SIR – The global IT outage involving CrowdStrike, Microsoft and others has thrown the UK’s dependence on Big Tech into sharp relief. We put all of our eggs in too few baskets and will be counting the economic consequences of this outage for a very long time.The Competition and Markets Authority’s (CMA) investigation into the dominance of Microsoft and Amazon Web Services (AWS) in the UK’s public cloud infrastructure market is a welcome, but long overdue, step. For example, the UK public sector’s heavy reliance on Microsoft and AWS for critical public services – from the NHS and HMRC to the Home Office, Ministry of Defence, and our intelligence services – creates a significant national security risk, as this most recent outage has reminded us.With Microsoft and AWS enjoying a combined UK market share of around 70-90 per cent, according to the CMA’s own research, the lack of competition presents a serious concern for our nation’s security and resilience. Should the CMA and the Government not be treating this as a matter of national importance? A robust national cloud strategy is essential to mitigate risk and foster a more diverse and resilient IT infrastructure.We need a clear plan that encourages competition, supports UK sovereign cloud providers, and ensures essential public services are not reliant on a handful of foreign companies.Simon HansfordFormer CEO, UKCloudEffingham, Surrey
SIR – It is ironic that the day after the lack of an adequate contingency plan for a global pandemic was highlighted by the Covid Inquiry, the world was hit by a significant failure of IT systems.The fact that so many organisations, such as the NHS, have been partially disabled seems to indicate that we are not well prepared.This IT outage was not the result of malign action; imagine how much worse that would be.Urgent action must be taken to devise, and have ready, appropriate contingency measures.Jos BinnsMilbourne, Wiltshire
SIR – Mathew Lynn is right (Business, July 20); we are overly dependent on computers. My wife and I ran a busy sub-post office during the three-day weeks of the 1970s and kept it open throughout. No computers then – just candles and cash to pay pensions and other benefits.Geoff NealeCheltenham, Gloucestershire
SIR – Many of the eight-year-olds that I teach only come into contact with cash when they are fortunate enough to be visited by the Tooth Fairy.I suspect that it is merely a matter of time before she too goes contactless. We will then have a whole generation growing up with no concept of coin recognition, or the real value of money.Catherine KidsonBradfield, Berkshire
SIR – As an ex-member of the Conservative Party, I despair at the choice of possible successors to Rishi Sunak. The two possible candidates put forward by readers (Letters, July 19), James Cleverly and Tom Tugendhat, do not inspire or appear to have the ability to offer the kind of leadership that will be needed to bring a divided parliamentary party together. Suella Braverman and Kemi Badenoch are the only possible candidates that have shown they understand the basics of Conservative principles.The fact remains whoever is elected will have to compete with Reform UK and its leader, Nigel Farage, who has an enviable reputation for political success and the kind of courage needed to take on an establishment that has a natural antipathy towards anything that hints at conservatism.D R TaylorLymington, Hampshire
Congratulations to President Joe Biden for stepping down in the US presidential race, clearly a difficult decision. Unfortunately, President Biden’s endorsed Kamala Harris now faces a gargantuan mountain to the White House. The Democrats need a candidate with kudos to triumph against Donald Trump and the only contender for that role is Michelle Obama.Chris Learmont-HughesCaldy, Wirral
SIR – Further to the letter from Jennifer Wade (July 20) about the ongoing 18-month closure of the only main road from the west of the city into Oxford, it should be noted that access to the station is almost impossible for commuters with mobility issues. Network Rail and Oxon County Council have been told that they are in breach of their legal duty under the Equality Act to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. They have been shown how access could be improved, but remain unresponsive. In 2016 I had the privilege of chairing a parliamentary inquiry into the Equality Act and its impact on disabled people. We noted the difficulties of enforcing rights against non-compliers and recommended that an ombudsman be given the specific duty of ensuring compliance. There are complaints procedures but they are slow and convoluted, with no guarantee of success at the end. Now that I am less mobile and find that Network Rail and Oxon CC are making my commute from west Oxford to the House of Lords very slow, difficult and painful, I can but urge the Government once again to provide a rapid enforcement mechanism to uphold the rights of disabled people in the provision of transport and other services.Baroness Deech (Crossbench)Oxford
SIR – May I thank Chris Thomas (Letters, July 20) for sharing the advice of the UK Tea and Infusions Association on the correct water temperature for brewing tea. I found by chance that using water just off the boil brews a more palatable, smooth cup of tea. I take my tea black, and shudder at anyone else making it. I love my mother dearly, but have to dilute the acrid treacle she usually brews.Tim BradburyNorthwich, Cheshire
SIR – It is interesting that amid all the furore surrounding Britain’s colonial past, the name of the woman who shamed the government into stopping its brutal treatment of the Boers and ending its war has not been mentioned. This is set to change with the recent opening of the Emily Hobhouse Museum, which uses immersive technology to take the visitor through the origins, conduct and conclusion of the South African campaigns just prior to the First World War. The museum is set in Emily’s birthplace, a beautiful rambling Victorian rectory in a tiny Cornish village not far from Liskeard. The story of this remarkable woman and her work is a must for any parents seeking to inspire their children with high ideals and teach them how, even in the most brutal of circumstances, these ideals can prevail to effect change.Denis WilkinsLiskeard, Cornwall
SIR – I once confused my pre-teenage sons when they took my list to do the shopping (Letters, July 17) when I was poorly.They came back saying that they had got everything but that one thing might not be right. I had written “sponge” with no explanation and they knew I made my own cakes and anyway, did I mean jam or chocolate? I had meant a sponge for cleaning the bath. Janet HainesReading, Berkshire
SIR – The Government’s rhetoric on house building is highly misleading. Let’s be quite clear: the Government is not going to build 1.5 million houses.Apart from building a few council houses, all the Government can do is to try to create conditions favourable to house building and hope that developers build more houses.Roger SimmensLyndhurst, Hampshire
SIR – Juxtaposed with Labour’s plans for new homes must be proper infrastructure: schools, surgeries and trading stores, plus access to trains and bus services. In the long term this will be money well invested. Homes should be to live in and not to invest in.Larry SequeiraCroydon, Surrey
SIR – I wonder if this Government realises that the Nimbys of today are the voters of tomorrow.Carol KellyHorwich, Lancashire
SIR – The prison sentences given to five Just Stop Oil protesters (report, July 19) are appropriate. The naturalist and presenter Chris Packham and Left-wing MPs inevitably condemn the sentences as unjust and an attack on peaceful protest. Depriving people of cancer treatment and of receiving vital medication is not peaceful. Causing physical harm, and the anguish of those unable to attend funerals, should not be dismissed. Let’s hope the sentences deter other fanatics from causing such harm.Jennie NaylorEast Preston, West Sussex
SIR – Chris Packham has described climate change as the most serious existential threat ever faced by the human species, with no shortage of scientific evidence to support this claim. Disruption to lives may be the least of our concerns unless the man-made causes of climate change are addressed far more vigorously. The protesters were driven by a sense of urgent desperation, believing that only direct action would impel decision-makers to act with the speed and conviction necessary to save this planet from an unprecedented disaster.The majority of us must accept some responsibility for this situation because of our own failure to take the threat seriously and believe that it will, if left unchecked, endanger future generations. We are reluctant to alter the lives we take for granted, and push to the back of our minds the consequences of failing to act. Governments must be far tougher. We must be helped, but also compelled, to change our lives now and understand why.David PlattsNewark, Nottinghamshire

Thanks for joining us today. Chris and I will be back on Monday to cover the latest from the markets, but I will leave you with Christopher Jasper’s report on how Deutsche Bahn, once synonymous with efficiency, is having a bad Euro 2024:
England football fans usually return home singing the praises of their host’s public transport. After a month crisscrossing Germany, they have a very different story to tell.
Once a byword for efficient travel, state railway Deutsche Bahn has been ravaged by years of underinvestment, leaving the network beset by delays, cancellations and overcrowding.
Euro 2024 has seen supporters, the media and even officials struggling to get to and from games – with trains failing to turn up, terminated without warning miles from their destination, or standing motionless for hours while chock full of frustrated passengers.
Such has been the level of disruption that even a four-day hiatus between England’s semi-final triumph in Dortmund and the potentially history-making clash with Spain 300 miles away in Berlin on Sunday offers no guarantee of a trouble-free journey.
Around 150,000 fans are forecast to descend on the German capital this weekend, some holding tickets for the final, others there to sample the atmosphere. In reality they may spend much of their time drinking in the ambience of a packed Deutsche Bahn platform or carriage.
Read the full story...
Angela Rayner is preparing to overhaul green rules that prevent house building in the countryside as Labour presses ahead with a promise to “bulldoze” the planning system. Melissa Lawford reports:
The Housing Secretary is gearing up to reform controversial so-called nutrient neutrality rules that are blocking hundreds of thousands of homes from being built, as part of Labour’s manifesto promise to add 1.5 million properties over this Parliament.
The plans could prove politically toxic for Ms Rayner after she opposed former Housing Secretary Michael Gove’s proposals to reform the rules last year, describing them as “reckless”. Mr Gove’s plans were eventually blocked by Labour in the House of Lords.
Jon Stoddart, head of London and South East planning at the property consultant CBRE, said: “They were pretty vociferous in their objection to it [in opposition]... you can see that being played back to Labour quite significantly.”
Read the full story...
European shares rose today and logged their second consecutive weekly gains on upbeat earnings and global investor optimism about a September interest rate cut by the US Federal Reserve.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 index closed up nearly 0.9pc, while the euro zone blue-chip gauge (the Euro Stoxx 50) advanced 1.3pc. Both indexes hit their highest levels in over a month on an intra-day basis.
A note from analysts at Bank of America Global Research said:
While a robust [second quarter] reporting season could provide further near-term support for Stoxx 600 EPS [earnings per share] momentum, we expect this to give way to renewed downgrades as global growth momentum weakens in response to the lagged impact of monetary tightening and the fading of support seen last year from US fiscal stimulus.
The FTSE 100 nudged upwards on Friday - driven higher by several utilities, housing and mining stocks.
The blue-chip index rose endeed the week at 8,253, a 0.4pc uplift.
Investors were buoyed this week by stronger-than-expected gross domestic product news in May on Thursday.
Early in the day, they had another boost amid growing hopes of a September interest rate cut by the Federal Reserve after US inflation data fell.
Danni Hewson, head of financial analysis at AJ Bell, said:
It’s hard to believe it has only been a week since Labour’s landslide election victory changed the UK’s political make-up.
There’s been no shortage of big announcements from Number 11 but the main economic news impacting London markets is rooted in the past, with faster than anticipated economic growth in May slashing expectation of an August interest rate cut by the Bank of England.
Add that to cooler than expected inflation over in the US and it’s created an economic stew that has boosted the value of the pound.
France’s CAC 40 finished 1.3pc up, while Germany’s Dax rose 1.2pc.
As the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq hover near record highs on Wall Street, investors are hoping for strong profit growth from companies beyond tech heavyweights such as Nvidia, so that the US stocks rally can broaden out.
Analysts expect second-quarter earnings for S&P 500 firms to grow by 9.6pc, from a decline of 2.8pc in the same period in 2023, according to LSEG IBES data.
The small-cap Russell 2000 rose 1.2pc to hit a six-month high today, while the S&P 400 Mid Cap index rose 1pc. The two indexes have lagged the S&P 500 this year.
Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group, said:
We think the rotation into the underloved, underappreciated, underperforming small- and mid-caps could take the baton in the second half of this year, as the Fed is clearly more dovish than they’ve been.
Global stock markets mostly powered ahead on Friday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average of 30 leading US companies breaking above 40,000 points. This represented a new record as traders increasingly expect the US Federal Reserve to cut interest rates.
Tokyo bucked the trend as the yen shot higher after a possible central bank intervention.
Wall Street’s main indexes advanced despite a lacklustre start of the earnings season, with bank shares taking a hit despite beating forecasts.
Shares in Wells Fargo tanked around 7pc as its retail banking activities flagged and its costs rose more than its revenue. Citigroup shares fell as much as 3.6pc, while JPMorgan Chase, the biggest US bank by assets, fell by 2.6pc.
The S&P 500 is up 0.7pc, the Dow Jones is up 0.8pc and the Nasdaq is up 0.8pc.
The yen hit an almost four-week high against the US dollar on Friday, raising speculation that Japanese authorities may have intervened for a second day to prop up the currency.
The rally in the Japanese currency, which has been languishing at around 38-year lows, began on Thursday just after data showed US consumer prices for June eased, boosting the odds of the Federal Reserve cutting rates as soon as September.
On Friday, the move came after data showed that US producer prices increased moderately in June.
Steve Englander of Standard Chartered in New York said:
If they intervened yesterday, it makes it likely that they intervened today. And I think it’s good strategy to keep the market off balance.
In what could be a further sign that pandemic-era working from home is well and truly over, it turns out that Spanish bank BBVA is on the lookout for a new London HQ - and it wants to nearly double its floorspace.
Bloomberg reported that it is looking for 50,00 square feet of space, up from 30,000 today.
BBVA currently has offices in Canary Wharf.
The FTSE 100 closed up 0.4pc today. The biggest riser was Rightmove, up 4pc, followed by industrial group Spirax, up 2.8pc. United Utilities was the biggest faller, down 3.4pc, followed by Endeavour Mining, down 2.3pc.
Meanwhile, the mid-cap FTSE 250 rose 0.1pc. The top riser was agricultural science business Genus, up 4.5pc, followed by Trustpilot, up by almost the same amount. The biggest faller was industrial business Dowlais, down 3.5pc, followed by office landlord Workspace, down 3.1pc.
Germany is set to abstain in Monday’s vote by European Union member states on imposing provisional tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), sources told Reuters today.
The European Union is imposing provisional tariffs of up to 37.6pc on EVs imported from China, ratcheting up tensions with Beijing in the EU’s largest trade case yet.
This first vote is not binding. This will be followed by a final vote after which the European Commission’s tariff proposal will be adopted unless there is qualified majority against it.
Yields of euro zone bonds rose slightly today after news that US producer price inflation was stronger than expected in June. They were, nonetheless, on track for a weekly fall after a sharp drop yesterday on the back of weak US consumer price data.
The German 10-year bond yield, the benchmark for the euro zone, was last up 3 basis points (bps) at 2.5pc, yet on track to end the week around 6 bps lower after dropping 7 bps on Thursday.
Year-on-year producer price index inflation rose to 2.6pc in June from 2.4pc in May, above economists’ expectations for a 2.3pc increase.
France’s 10-year bond yield, which has been in focus after Sunday’s election resulted in a hung parliament, rose 3 bps to 3.155pc but was on track to finish the week 6 bps lower.
The spread between French and German borrowing costs was steady at 65 bps.
The European Central Bank will meet to set interest rates next week, although traders think another rate cut after June’s reduction is highly unlikely.
The Russian president Vladimir Putin has today signed a bill into law that scraps what is left of so-called “flat tax” that was once enthusiastically endorsed by Western free-marketeers.
The change raises income taxes for the rich, part of efforts to help fill government coffers during Russia’s war in Ukraine.
The legislation, which envisages a progressive tax on personal income, is a major change from the 13pc flat-rate tax that was widely credited with improving revenue collections after it was introduced in 2001.
The Adam Smith Institute has said that Russia’s flat tax produced “remarkable results”, with flat taxes said to boost economic growth.
Richard Teather, a tax specialist who writes for the Adam Smith Institue, explained that: “One of the reasons for Russia’s adoption of the flat tax was its high level of avoidance under the earlier multi-rate system”.
However, in 2021, Russia modified the system so that people earning more than 5m rubles (£43,200) a year would pay 15pc on the amount above the threshold. It effectively kept the flat tax for most workers.
Mr Putin has said that the tax increase would affect no more than 3.2pc of Russia’s taxpayers.
The new law means Russians will pay a 13pc tax for incomes of up to 2.4m rubles (£20,900) a year. For incomes over that amount, a steadily higher tax rate would apply, with the maximum rate of 22pc for incomes exceeding 50m rubles ($435,000).
The bill also hikes the rate of corporation tax from 20pc to 25pc.
The US stock market rally - fuelled by the Big Tech firms such as Nvidia and Apple - is “broadening out”, an analyst has said.
Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, said:
Market breadth is improving and this is why the Russell 2000, the US mid cap index, has surged this week and is currently at its highest level since early 2022. This suggests that for the second day, the stock market rally is broadening out, at the same time as expectations for interest rate cuts are surging in the US.
The market expects the Fed to cut rates in September, and there is now a 95pc probability of a rate cut, even though producer prices were stronger than expected.
However, this stage of the monetary policy cycle could be tricky for the banks, which may explain why they are selling off at the end of the week.
As we mentioned earlier, the euro has slumped to its lowest level against the pound in nearly two years as traders compared the political stability in Britain compared to that of its neighbour France.
The boost to the pound came after better-than-expected British growth figures were released on Thursday. They showed that the economy in the past three months grew at the fastest pace in more than two years. It expanded by 0.9pc in the three months to May.
The pound was also helped by a slowdown in American inflation which suggested that the world’s largest economy could cut interest rates earlier than the UK, making the pound a more attractive currency to hold.
Analysts say that market scepticism shown towards the UK is fading away, with the pound now a whisker away from the psychologically significant $1.30 level. Goldman has now predicted that it could reach that level within two weeks.
Today, the pound is up 0.5pc against the dollar at $1.2988 and up 0.2pc against the euro at €1.1914.
“It’s a huge change compared to how hated it was,” said Janet Mui, head of market analysis at RBC Brewin Dolphin.
Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, said: “The growth outlook is brighter and the real interest-rate differential is there. The pound is not seen as a risky currency any more.”
Meanwhile, uncertainty around the direction of French politics continues to weigh down on the euro.
Michael Hart, senior currency strategist at Pictet Wealth Management, said: “One may or may not agree with the Labour programme, but at least there’s some clarity there … We are positive on the pound in the near term.”
Shahab Jalinoos, global head of foreign exchange research at UBS Investment Bank, told the FT: “Simply shifting the narrative towards a more energetic drive for change could, on the margin, be helpful for both investment and growth.”
He said that Britain “arguably the most stable government in the G7 over the next five years”, so the pound “should finally see the tide of structural flows move in its favour for the first time in the post-Brexit-vote era”.
Global stock markets have mostly advanced today as traders increasingly expect the US Federal Reserve to cut interest rates.
Tokyo bucked the trend as the yen shot higher on expectations of a possible central bank intervention. The Nikkei 225 fell 2.5pc.
Wall Street’s main indexes rose at the opening bell despite bank shares taking a hit at the start of the earnings season despite beating forecasts. The S&P 500 is up 0.8pc, the Dow is up 0.5pc and the Nasdaq is up 1.1pc.
In Europe, the Stoxx 600 is up 0.9pc, while France’s Cac 40 is up 1.4pc and Germany’s Dax us up 1.1pc.
African countries have asked World Trade Organisation chief Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala to run for a second term as the head of the global trade watchdog, a document showed on Friday.
Okonjo-Iweala, a former Nigerian finance minister, made history by becoming the first female and African chief of the 30-year-old trade body in 2021. Her term formally ends in August 2025 and she has not yet commented publicly on her plans.
“The African Group is of the view that it would be in the best interest of the Organisation if the process of reappointment were to start early,” according to the document sent by Chad, asking Okonjo-Iweala to make herself available for reappointment.
Under WTO rules, Ms Okonjo-Iweala, 70, has until the end of November to decide whether to apply.
Some WTO delegates have privately speculated that she may want to avoid a second term if US presidential candidate Donald Trump wins in November, since his administration opposed her appointment.
Ms Okonjo-Iweala has also previously voiced concerns that some of Mr Trump’s proposals could upend the global trading system.
I will bid you farewell for the week at this point and pass the baton to Alex Singleton, who will keep the live updates coming.
Good luck to England at the weekend as they chase glory against Spain in the Euros. It could be a tricky start to the week on Monday for many people if the Three Lions bring football home.
Also bringing it home this week was Liam Nicholson, 27, who was first in line to buy Apple’s Vision Pro augmented reality headset at its Regent Street store in London.
The device went on sale in Britain for the first time today, with Mr Nicholson the first in as the doors opened at 8am.
He said trying out the tech was a “really good experience” and thought it was worth the money. Prices start at £3,499.
Oil have edged higher for a third day amid increasing bets that the US Federal Reserve will begin cutting interest rates in September.
Brent crude rose 0.2pc near $86 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate climbed 0.4pc to nearly $83.
While data on Thursday indicated US inflation has eased, wholesale prices rose slightly more than expected today.
International benchmark Brent had gained as much as 1.1pc before the producer prices data was released.
Either way, markets are pricing in a rate cut by the Fed in September, which lowers the relative value of the dollar, pushing up the price of oil, which is measured in the US currency.
A state-backed nuclear laboratory at the heart of Britain’s proposed mini-reactor revolution is facing closure in a headache for new Energy Secretary Ed Miliband.
Our energy editor Jonathan Leake has the details:
Researchers and staff at Sheffield University’s Nuclear Advanced Manufacturing Research Centre (AMRC) have been warned of possible redundancies amid a major overhaul.
The centre, which employs about 150 people, is focused on engineering the specialist steel needed to build small modular reactors (SMRs) – a key element of Britain’s strategy to quadruple nuclear power by 2050.
Staff have been told that only about 30 of them will be retained and they will be absorbed into the larger university-run Advanced Manufacturing Research Centre, which employs about 700 workers.
Read what the AMRC closure means for Britain.
US stock indexes edged higher at the opening bell despite investors booking profits in tech heavyweights and wholesale inflation proving stronger than expected.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 29.5 points, or 0.1pc, at the open to 39783.28.
The S&P 500 rose 6.2 points, or 0.1pc at the open to 5590.76​, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 20.2 points, or 0.1pc, to 18303.641 at the opening bell.
Gold prices have fallen after stronger-than-expected US wholesale inflation dampened hopes for interest rate cuts in September.
Bullion fell as much as 1pc to below $2,400 an ounce, after climbing 1.9pc on Thursday following the slowest growth in US core inflation since 2021.
Traders are now pricing in a September interest rate cut by the Federal Reserve but have slightly scaled back their bets after the producer prices index - which measures wholesale inflation - rose more than expected to 2.6pc.
Gold has rallied 16pc this year to reach a record $2,450.07 in May amid heightened geopolitical risks and strong buying by central banks.
The euro has slumped to its lowest level against the pound in nearly two years amid the contrasting political stability in Britain compared to neighbour France.
Sterling was up 0.2pc against the euro, making it worth less than 84p, its lowest point since August 2022.
After US wholesale inflation rose more than expected last month, Paul Ashworth of Capital Economics said:
Ignore the fact that core PPI increased by a slightly bigger-than-expected 0.4pc month-on-month in June and that May was revised to a 0.3pc rise from unchanged.
The PPI components that feed into the Fed’s preferred PCE deflator inflation measure were significantly lower than expected for June and it looks like May’s PCE gain could be revised down too, albeit only slightly.
The big news is that, after applying our own seasonal adjustment, PPI hospital prices increased by only 0.1pc month-on-month in June and the massive 1.3pc month-on-month surge in May was revised down to a 0.6pc gain.
Mr Ashworth added that the latest data meant that a September rate cut was “on the way – and we can’t completely rule out a surprise move in July”.
Carpetright is on the verge of calling in administrators, as the retail chain races to find a buyer amid fears for almost 2,000 jobs.
The company, which has around 270 stores, has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators amid a scramble to shore up new investment.
Advisory firm PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) has been lined up for the role.
Kevin Barrett, chief executive of Carpetright owner Nestware Holdings, said: “We remain focussed on securing external investment to ensure as few customers and colleagues are impacted as possible.
“They are our main priority and we are taking all appropriate action to make sure they are informed and supported through this process. We have begun promising conversations with interested parties that are moving in the right direction, encouraging us that Carpetright has a viable future.”
It comes after it emerged earlier this week that Carpetright had put itself up for sale amid concerns over cashflow.
Carpetright has been hit by a slowdown in sales, as pressures on households mean fewer people are spending on new floors. It was also dealt a blow in April when a cyber attack left it unable to trade.
The notice of intention to appoint administrators gives it ten days protection, allowing it to hold talks with potential suitors.
Wholesale inflation unexpectedly rose in the US last month in a blow to hopes of swift interest rate cuts.
A day after consumer prices data put a spring in the step of markets, the latest producer prices index climbed to 2.6pc in June, which was higher than the 2.3pc predicted by analysts.
The reading for May was also revised higher from 2.2pc to 2.4pc, according to the Labor Department.
As a result, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq turned lower in premarket trading.
Ahead of the opening bell, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up eight points, or less than 0.1pc, the S&P 500 was down 4.75 points, or 0.1pc, and the Nasdaq 100 had fallen 36.25 points, or 0.2pc.
German airline Lufthansa has slashed its profit forecast after a weak second quarter, and warned it would be “challenging” for its flagship carrier to break even.
The flagship carrier for Europe’s largest economy said it now expects operating profit of €1.4bn to €1.8bn (£1.2bn to £1.5bn) for the year, down from a previous estimate of around €2.2bn (£1.9bn).
Total second-quarter operating profit at Lufthansa - which also runs Eurowings, Austrian, Swiss and Brussels Airlines - was €686m, down from €1.1bn a year earlier.
Lufthansa Airlines saw its profits fall particularly sharply due to a “negative market trend”, inefficient flight operations and delayed aircraft delivery.
It said: “It is becoming increasingly challenging for Lufthansa Airlines to break even for the full year.
“To counteract this, a comprehensive turnaround program is being launched.”
Citigroup’s profit rose in the second quarter after a 60pc jump in investment banking revenue and gains in its services division.
Net income at the third largest US lender climbed to $3.2bn (£2.5bn), or $1.52 per share, in the three months to the end of June, compared with $2.9bn (£2.2bn), or $1.33 per share, a year earlier.
The results come two days after US regulators fined Citi $136m for making “insufficient progress” in fixing data management problems identified in 2020.
Regulators also required the lender to demonstrate it was putting enough resources toward those efforts.
Citi had already booked the penalties and additional investments on the data work in the second quarter.
Chief executive Jane Fraser is carrying out a sweeping overhaul in an effort to improve the bank’s performance, cut costs and simplify its sprawling businesses.
As part of the turnaround, Citi aims to shrink its workforce by 20,000 over the next two years.
AT&T has admitted it suffered a massive hacking incident as data from about 109m customer accounts containing records of calls and texts from 2022 was illegally downloaded in April.
The US telecom company said the FBI is investigating and at least one person has been arrested after AT&T call logs were copied from its workspace on a third-party cloud platform in a significant breach of consumer communication records.
AT&T said the compromised data includes files containing AT&T records of calls and texts of nearly all of AT&T’s cellular and AT&T’s landline customers interacting with those cellular numbers between May 2022 and October 2022 but does not contain the content of calls or texts or personal information such as social security numbers.
AT&T shares were down 2pc in premarket trading.
The compromised data also includes records from January 2, 2023, for a very small number of customers.
JP Morgan Chase set aside more money to cover bad loans as it reported higher second-quarter profits thanks to better results in investment banking.
Profits at the big US bank came in at $18.1bn (£14bn), up 25pc from the year-ago period. The earnings were boosted by a $7.9bn gain from a share-exchange transaction with Visa.
Revenues rose 22pc to $50.2bn as the lender, the biggest US bank by assets, pointed to a boost from higher investment banking fees and asset management fees, as well as a lift from greater net interest income (NII).
NII is based on the interest JPMorgan earns on loans less the interest it pays out to depositors.
However, profits were dampened by higher costs for bad loans, sending shares down 1.5pc in premarket trading.
The provision for credit losses rose 5pc to $3.1bn (£2.4bn), with JPMorgan citing credit cards as a driver of both charge-offs in the latest quarter and reserves over future potential losses.
Chief executive Jamie Dimon said the bank had performed “well” in the quarter, but reiterated his concerns about the outlook.
He said: “While market valuations and credit spreads seem to reflect a rather benign economic outlook, we continue to be vigilant about potential tail risks.”
Consumer goods giant Unilever plans to cut a third of its office roles in Europe by the end of next year, it has been reported, amid pressure from activist investors to boost returns.
The FTSE 100-listed owner of brands like Dove and Hellmann’s told senior executives this week that it would axe as many as 3,200 jobs across the continent by the end of 2025, according to the Financial Times.
The company has come under pressure from shareholders like activist investor Nelson Peltz, announcing plans earlier this year to sell its ice cream business.
It is undergoing a  “productivity programme” first announced in March that will involve as many as 7,500 job cuts around the world.
Its share price has risen by more than 15pc so far this year.
Airlines are putting on extra flights as tens of thousands of England football fans travel to Germany for the Euro 2024 final.
British Airways said it will operate two additional flights from Heathrow to Berlin on Sunday, where England’s match against Spain takes place at 8pm.
This will boost the carrier’s seat capacity for travel to the German capital by “nearly 30%pc”, a spokesman said.
Extra capacity has also been added for return flights on Monday to bring fans home.
British Airways saw a surge in demand for air travel to Berlin following England’s semi-final victory over the Netherlands on Wednesday night, peaking 11 minutes after the final whistle at 10.05pm.
Ryanair announced it will operate two extra return flights from Stansted to Berlin, departing on Sunday and returning on Monday.
The airline’s head of communications Jade Kirwan said: “To facilitate the unprecedented demand from England fans looking to cheer on the Three Lions in Berlin this Sunday, we’ve added over 1,500 extra seats between London Stansted and Berlin.”
The Bank of England will wait until November before it begins to cut interest rates, HSBC has predicted, amid concerns that Labour will fuel inflation by announcing more rises in the minimum wage.
The lender delayed its forecast for the first reduction in the borrowing costs for four years, having previously said the move would happen in August.
Money markets indicate there is a 50pc chance of a rate cut when policymakers meet next month.
Interest rates have stood at 5.25pc - their highest level in 16 years - since August last year.
Economist Liz Martins wrote in a note to clients: “The upcoming decisions are likely to be ‘finely balanced’.
“We see wage growth and inflation remaining sticky, particularly if Labour’s plans include another sizeable hike to the National Living Wage in April 2025.”
Action in the foreign exchange market in the last 24 hours has been dominated by the yen, which rose by the most since early May on Thursday.
It comes after the Bank of Japan likely intervened to prop it up, just as the dollar weakened following a softer US inflation report.
The pound dropped by over 1pc against the yen on Thursday, as the Japanese currency strengthened broadly.
It was last up 0.3pc at 205.65 yen, near its highest since early 2008.
Twitter is misleading users with its blue ticks for certified accounts, Brussels has said, in a ruling that leaves Elon Musk’s social media platform facing heavy fines for violating EU content rules.
The social network “deceives” users with its blue badges since anyone can now obtain one, the European Commission said.
The EU said the availability of blue ticks was impacting “users’ ability to make free and informed decisions”.
Brussels also found that Twitter, now known as X, broke rules related to transparency on advertising and giving researchers’ access to public data.
The pound has jumped to its highest level this year as traders ramp up bets on US interest rate cuts.
Sterling has gained 0.3pc to $1.295, its highest point since July 2023, after money markets priced in a first quarter of a point reduction by the Federal Reserve in September.
Kit Juckes, chief FX strategist at Societe Generale, said currency markets “will probably assume a base case of rate cuts in both the UK and US in September, but the stickiness of UK inflation could translate into a further push higher in GBP/USD”.
He added: “The UK’s inflation stickiness is not, however, something to cheer about, but a side effect of ‘doing’ Brexit at the beginning of a global pandemic that caused enough supply-side price shocks without any additional help from politicians.”
Ozempic, the diabetes drug that has become a global sensation because of its weight-loss benefits, has been linked to lower rates of dementia, according to an Oxford University study.
The treatment, made by Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk, lowered the risk of dementia in patients by 48pc compared to an older drug, the research published in the Lancet said.
Taking Ozempic also resulted in a 28pc lower risk of smoking compared to those taking glipozide, the study showed.
Novo Nordisk shares were up 0.3pc this morning.
Apple’s Vision Pro headset, which blends the real world with digital content in front of the wearer’s eyes, has gone on sale in the UK for the first time.
The “spatial computing” device - which is in essence a wearable computer that overlaps apps and other content on top of the real world - starts at £3,499 and is controlled by the user’s eyes, hands and voice.
A small queue of seven eager fans waited outside Apple’s flagship Regent Street store in London this morning as enthusiasts across the country got a taste of the first-of-its-kind device.
Liam Nicholson, 27, who was first in line as the doors opened at 8am, said trying out the tech was a “really good experience” and thought it was worth the money.
Rumi Onoda, 50, was the first person to purchase the headset from the Regent Street store, which she said felt “immersive” and left her “speechless”.
“I feel like I’m in a sci-fi film,” she added.
Customers who booked in advance had the opportunity to test the Vision Pro for free in-store with the assistance of Apple staff who helped them adjust to using finger gestures and eye movements to alter the environment around them.
The new head of banking at Citigroup has been awarded about $41m (£31.7m) worth of shares in the lender after being poached from rival JPMorgan.
Viswas Raghavan, 57, who reports directly to chief executive Jane Fraser, received 623,838 shares, regulatory documents show.
Citigroup’s stock closed at $65.71 on Thursday.
It replaces the compensation Mr Raghavan gave up when he switched to Citi from JP Morgan.
He will be given the shares in six installments from January 2026 to 2031, none of which is eligible for immediate sale.
Swedish inflation fell to its lowest level in almost three years in June, official figures showed, increasing the likelihood of an interest rate cut.
Consumer prices in the Scandinavian country rose by 2.6pc in June, down from 3.7pc in May, according to Statistics Sweden.
The agency noted it was the lowest reading of the consumer price index since September 2021.
The inflation measure used by Sweden’s central bank to guide monetary policy, which is adjusted for interest rates, fell to 1.3pc, well below its 2pc inflation target.
The Riksbank left its main interest rate unchanged in late June at 3.75pc after it made its first cut in eight years in May.
But the central bank said that the rate could “be cut two or three times during the second half of the year,” if inflation continued to ease.
After a series of rate hikes aimed at reining in inflation, Sweden’s interest rate had been held at four percent since September 2023, its highest level since 2008.

The FTSE 100 hit a one-week high as investors cheered growing bets of a September interest rate cut by the Federal Reserve after a surprise fall in US inflation data.
The blue-chip FTSE 100 index was up 0.3pc, while the domestically-focused mid-cap FTSE 250 was little changed after closing at a more than two-year high on Thursday.
Both indexes are on track to log their second weekly gains.
Investor sentiment was buoyed globally by increased bets of an interest rate cut by the Fed in September, after data showed a surprise drop in US consumer prices for June on Thursday.
London’s pharmaceutical and biotech stocks rose as much as 1.6pc, while medical equipment and services shares gained as much as 1.1pc.
Precious metal miners sunk to the bottom with a 0.7pc decline in tandem with gold prices.
The market’s focus is now on the producer prices data in the US that could further strengthen the case for rate cuts in September.
Meanwhile, Ashmore dipped 3.9pc to the bottom of the FTSE 250 after the fund manager reported a further $2bn (£1.6bn) of quarterly net outflows of client cash, as investors continued to shun its emerging markets funds.
Wholesale gas prices are on track for their biggest weekly slump in two months amid fading concerns about supplies.
Dutch front-month futures, Europe’s benchmark contract, have dropped about 6pc since Monday - the biggest decline since April - as traders rebuild stocks ahead of the winter.
Europe’s gas storage sites are 80pc full, which is higher than normal for the time of the year.
Meanwhile, mild weather is reducing demand for air conditioning and supplies from top producer Norway have been steady.
European gas prices were down 0.7pc today to less than €31 per megawatt hour. The UK equivalent was down 1.1pc to 71.4p per therm.
Ashmore revealed its clients pulled $2bn (£1.6bn) of their money from the emerging markets investor as they became more wary of riskier investments.
The London-listed fund revealed its assets under management shrank by $2.4bn in the three months to June as it was also hit by a $400m drop in the performance of its portfolio.
Shares dropped by as much as 3.6pc.
Chief executive Mark Coombs said:
Emerging markets have demonstrated resilience over the past few years, with effective monetary and fiscal policies underpinning superior GDP growth.
Further growth is supported by structural economic reforms in many emerging countries.
In contrast, the developed world faces numerous headwinds following a period of pro-cyclical fiscal expansion and a sharp increase in the cost of government debt.
As the trajectories of emerging and developed countries continue to diverge, investor appetite for emerging markets exposure will improve and capital flows will follow, supporting higher risk-adjusted returns in emerging markets over the medium term.
The FTSE 100 has opened higher as investors continued to be encouraged by figures showing the UK economy grew faster than expected in May.
The blue-chip index gained 0.6pc to 8,273.93 as trading began while the FTSE 250 was little changed at 21,193.12.
The Federal Reserve will begin cutting interest rates in September, money markets indicate, after US inflation continued to slow down.
Traders are pricing in a quarter of a percentage point cut at the September meeting of Fed policymakers after the consumer prices index dropped from 3.3pc to 3pc in June, which was a sharper decline than expected.
The pound jumped to its highest level against the dollar in a year to more than $1.29 while US government borrowing costs also dropped.
The two-year Treasury bond yield - the return the government promises to pay buyers of its debts - fell by the largest amount since January.
Deutsche Bank analyst Jim Reid said: “Of course, it’s worth remembering that one report doesn’t make a trend, but recent months have brought some of the weakest inflation numbers since the current surge began in 2021, and it’s led to growing expectations that the Fed will finally be able to start cutting rates in the months ahead.”
China’s imports unexpectedly declined last month, official figures showed, as weakening consumption continues to plague its economy.
Imports dropped 2.3pc, according to China’s customs department, reversing May’s 1.8pc growth and much worse than the 2.5pc expected.
Meanwhile, its exports rose sharply in June as Beijing battles to kick start lacklustre growth.
Overseas sales of products and services overseas surged 8.6pc, up from 7.6pc in May and better than the 8pc forecast.
Zhiwei Zhang, chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said:
This reflects the economic condition in China, with weak domestic demand and strong production capacity relying on exports.
The sustainability of strong exports is a major risk for China’s economy in the second half of the year.
Economists at Goldman Sachs warned of “downside risks to exports in 2025 and 2026” if former US president Donald Trump is re-elected in November and slaps “large tariffs on all imports of Chinese goods, as he has suggested in recent months”.
Tesla shares have sunk after it reportedly pushed back the unveiling of its self-driving taxis.
The electric car maker’s shares were down 1.8pc in premarket trading following an 8.4pc plunge on Thursday, which was its largest fall since January.
It comes as Elon Musk’s car maker is pushing back the big-reveal of its so-called Robotaxis from August to October, according to Bloomberg News.
In recent months, Tesla’s chief executive has tried to reposition the company, pitching it as not simply another EV manufacturer but as a leader in self-driving technology.
As a paid-for software upgrade, it has the potential to dramatically improve Tesla’s profits compared to the famously tight margins of the car making industry.
Renting cars out as autonomous taxis would also present a new line of business: Uber without the need to pay a driver.

The yen swung between losses and gains in volatile trade, reflecting investors’ skittishness after Tokyo was thought to have intervened to prop up the Japanese currency in the wake of a cooler-than-expected US inflation report.
Moves in the yen against the dollar and other major currencies stole the spotlight on Friday, though in the broader market Asian stocks were headed for a weekly gain on growing bets for a September rate cut from the Federal Reserve.
The dollar was last 0.1pc higher at 159.10 yen, after rising more than 0.3pc to an intraday high of 159.45 yen and falling 0.7pc to a low of 157.75 yen in early trading
Moves were similarly choppy in the other yen crosses though subsided over the course of the trading day, with the euro last 0.2pc higher against the yen and sterling up 0.2pc, both reversing early losses.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.title: The £1.7 billion road that will never get built
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.subtitle: To campaigners it was a ‘monstrous project’, to locals a chance to end their traffic hell: this week Rachel Reeves consigned it to history
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.text:
Rachel Reeves delivered the coup de grace in the House of Commons on Monday afternoon. “The government has agreed not to move forward with projects that the previous government refused to publicly cancel despite knowing full well they were unaffordable,” said the Chancellor, adding that “that includes proposed works on the A303 and the A27.”
Every road user in the country knew instantly what she meant: the proposed tunnel under Stonehenge, one of the longest-running and most keenly debated road-building projects in British history, was off for good. Later the Government clarified in a post on Gov.uk that it was “cancelling” the A303 Stonehenge Tunnel, which at a cost of £1.7bn, was deemed a “low value, unaffordable scheme.”
It was a triumphant moment for the thousands who opposed the project, which is the latest in a long history of attempts to solve appalling traffic around the World Heritage site. “This is wonderful news,” said the historian Tom Holland, president of the Stonehenge Alliance. In recent years, Holland has become the tunnel’s most prominent opponent. He is the face of a resistance which has seen the project snared up in legal challenges and other objections.
“This entire monstrous project, a proposal to drive a gash of concrete and tarmac through our most sacred prehistoric landscape, should never have got off the drawing board,” Holland said.
His thoughts were echoed by other campaigners. Ami McCarthy, of Greenpeace UK, said: “ditching expensive white elephant road building schemes, which have been long fought by many local campaigners, is a wise move.”
For those who had supported the proposals, especially those living in areas around the neolithic site, however, it was disastrous news. They fear it will condemn them to terrible traffic for the rest of their lives – given drivers are routinely re-routed off the A303 by modern navigation systems and into the surrounding countryside – as well as taking away the chance to “reunite” the ancient landscape which surrounds the monument, which at present is divided by the trunk road.
“I’m gutted,” says Mark Verbinnen, a councillor for nearby Amesbury East and Bulford. “It has been moving forward and it was due to start this year. I had my suspicions when it got taken to the High Court again earlier this year. With the election and new government, I thought it could be the end. So I’m not surprised, but I’m very disappointed.
“Not just personally, but for a lot of the residents I represent, who have been crying out for a solution for the A303 for years, because of the sheer volume of traffic. On a nice sunny day these villages are overrun with traffic, by people whose satnavs pull them off the main road and through the villages. Every time there’s a crash or an accident, or even just a slow road, it’s hell to live here. I’m only 34, and this tunnel project has existed as long as I’ve been alive.”
The Conservative leader of Wiltshire County Council, Richard Clewer, was unequivocal in his criticism of the decision to cancel the project.
“I’m extremely cross with it,” he said. “It takes a scheme that was going to address one of the major traffic problems in the UK [...] in a very sensitive landscape. And after decades of work it’s all been pulled away at the very last minute.” Clewer added that £160m had already been spent on the scheme, with builders on site, laying the electricity cables that would have powered the boring machines.
“More importantly, the current government is going on about the need for economic growth,” he said. “Nothing drives economic growth more in terms of government investment than improvements fixing road problems. The A303 here blocks up the entirety of south-west England. Access by road to the south-west is really bad. By addressing this, which is the worst bottle-neck on that route, it would have done a great deal to unlock more economic growth.”
The government first tried to get to grips with the Stonehenge issue in the early 1990s. Compounding the problems posed by the sheer number of visitors the site receives, as it passes the structure on Salisbury Plain, the A303 drops down from a dual carriageway to a single-lane in each direction.
Drivers naturally slow down to look at the monument, made up of sarsens and bluestones, which causes further congestion and adds to the risk of accidents occuring. In the satnav era, this means cars are rerouted through neighbouring villages which are ill-equipped to handle the traffic.
Several solutions have been put forward, though none have ever come to fruition. The first tunnel, a shallower cut-and-cover proposal, was rejected after a public consultation in 1993. English Heritage and the National Trust returned with another idea for a deeper tunnel, but that was rejected as unaffordable in 1998. The Department of Transport tried again, with a slightly different design, four years later. That, too, was dropped in 2007, only to be revived by David Cameron in 2014.
After endless to’ing and fro’ing, while stakeholders considered everything from traffic, pollution, water tables, bat and butterfly populations, pollution and archaeology, planners eventually settled on a 1.8 mile version of the tunnel, a compromise that even at the time was nobody’s ideal solution. (Some preferred a longer tunnel, others rerouting the road further to the south, and there were those who were in favour of leaving things altogether.) The £1.7bn scheme was announced by ministers in 2017 and approved three years later, against the advice of the government’s Planning Inspectorate, which had recommended that Grant Shapps, the then Transport Secretary, withhold consent.
The decision was blocked by a High Court ruling in 2021, only for the project to be given the green light again in 2023, under Mark Harper’s stewardship of the Department for Transport. A subsequent bid to have the approval overturned again failed in a second High Court hearing held in February of this year.
Professor Michael Paker Pearson, an archaeologist specialising in Stonehenge who has been one of the leading voices in the Stonehenge Alliance, says that had the government listened to its own advice, the present situation could have been avoided. “The government’s planning inspectors turned down the scheme years ago because of the unacceptable damage it would cause,” he says. “If only the government had listened to their own experts they wouldn’t have wasted so much money.”
For some, the whole idea of a tunnel was flawed in the first place. “One of the few real pleasures in this life is the view of Stonehenge from the A303,” says Tom Fort, author of The A303: Highway to the Sun (2012), a book about the road, which runs from Hampshire to Devon. “Stonehenge is a rather underwhelming site. All you get close-up is a bigger version of what you see far away. What’s wonderful about it is its setting in the landscape and the mystery that endures when you look at it. You get that from the road: you see it in context.”
Still, he concedes that the cancellation is hard on local residents. “If you build the tunnel you push the traffic past Stonehenge but unless you dual carriageway the whole road, you’re transferring logjam from one place to another,” Fort says. “The people I feel sorry for are those who live in Winterbourne Stoke. Their lives have been blighted since the road was built. If there was any justice they’d have had a bypass. I think what’s awful for people living round there is the way hopes have been raised and dashed over and over again.”
If the locals are unhappy with Reeves’ decision, so are the organisations that had led the campaign for a new road. In a statement, English Heritage, which is responsible for Stonehenge, said it had been a “strong supporter of the tunnel project, which would reunite the ancient landscape and allow more people to explore and enjoy this remarkable site”. It added that it would “seek further dialogue with the government to find a solution.”
Meanwhile Duncan Wilson, chief executive of Historic England, said: “We understand the government needs to make difficult decisions on public spending, but we are disappointed by the decision to cancel the A303 Stonehenge Improvement Scheme.” He added that they “remain hopeful that at some point in the future this scheme could be reconsidered as the best option to solve the longstanding traffic issues around Stonehenge and reunite this internationally important prehistoric landscape.”
This week, that may be the only crumb of consolation for those who were keen on the tunnel. Thirty years is a long time in planning applications, but it is the blink of an eye for Stonehenge.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/news.title: Victoria Starmer’s Downing Street dress – and her message to the British middle class
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/news.subtitle: The Me+Em fit-and-flare dress cost £275, a price point widely acknowledged in the fashion industry as a middle-class sweet spot
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/news.text:
The real election winner has been Me+Em. Never mind wide but shallow support. The extremely successful, independent British brand, with 11 UK stores and two more recently opened in New York City, was founded in 2009, in the dying days of the last Labour government, by Clare Hornby and Emma Howarth.
Over the past 24 hours, it has won 100 per cent approval from Lady Starmer, who wore a £295 cream short sleeve single breasted jacket from the spring collection to the count last night, followed up with a £275 red (of course) fit-and-flare dress from the brand’s latest “drop”, and a pair of £295 silver slingbacks from Russell and Bromley, also a UK stalwart brand, to walk into Downing Street with her husband on Friday lunchtime.
So many key questions spring forth – ones you probably won’t find Laura Kuenssberg and her colleagues addressing. Is £295 henceforth a new Labour fiscal policy? It has been widely acknowledged in the fashion industry as a middle-class sweet spot – i.e., high enough to make an item seem reassuringly aspirational, but not obscenely so.
Also, is anyone styling, guiding or otherwise personal shopping for Lady Starmer, who, ever since we have seen her in public, has not put a sartorial foot wrong?
It is never easy dressing for a life of public scrutiny as a woman. When you are as private as Victoria Starmer, determined not to drown in her husband’s wake, it is doubly so. The former solicitor, as we all know, is an occupational health worker for the NHS and has two teenage children, who in accordance with their wishes, did not accompany their parents on their progress up the famous street.
Also, to judge from all the glad-handing and air-kissing that went on between her and the aides outside her new home, she has not been as disengaged from her husband’s career as reports have suggested. So when on Earth does she find time to shop; let alone work out an appropriate approach to public dressing and squeeze in the impressive-but-not-Penny-Mordaunt-scale blow dries that are already becoming a hallmark of her public appearances?
Perhaps she was always naturally stylish. Her strapless wedding dress from 2007 when her future husband was plain old Keir, is a good indicator that this may indeed be the case. It really hasn’t dated.
Vic, as her husband likes to call her, is a dab hand at finding a timeless, on-point outfit and seems too familiar with relatively unknown labels not to have an innate interest in fashion. Take the red cotton pintucked shirt dress she wore to vote yesterday – from Jonathan Simkhai, a New York-born designer who won US Vogue’s fashion fund prize back in 2015 and has a knack for clean, classic, American sportswear.
That dress, in a new, green iteration currently costs £445. Perhaps Lady Starmer bought hers a while ago at around the £295 mark. Perhaps she simply realises that investing a reasonable amount in what she wears is, at this stage in her life, a sensible use of her budget.
Further clues that Lady Starmer enjoys and understands the potential power of clothes: the bead-edged pale pink bias-cut dress she wore to a State banquet at Buckingham Palace in 2022 – fashionably vintage-looking; the sparkly cream number from Needle & Thread, a small British favourite of the Princess of Wales she wore to last week’s Japan State Banquet, and the red, belted Edeline Lee dress she wore to Party Conference last year. Lee, another favourite of the Princess, is a Canadian-born designer who makes every one of her flattering dresses in small batches at her East London studio, thus supporting jobs here and minimising waste.
Cast your mind back to that 1997 picture of a bleary Cherie Blair answering the doorbell of Number 10 in a cotton nightie from Next and ask yourself whether that could ever happen now.
The truth is, that ever since her husband began his rise to Number 10, Lady Starmer’s outfits will likely have been run through some kind of approval poll algorithm, carefully vetted for price, appropriateness and potential to offend someone somewhere, be it Just Stop Oil or The Natural Born KillJoy party. The fact that she hasn’t yet, is miracle enough. Let’s hope she can continue to shine a light on British brands of all sizes – because boy, it’s tough out there for business right now.
Lady Starmer, your country’s fashion industry needs you.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.title: Monty Don is a green radical mugged by gardening reality
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.subtitle: The allure of a freshly-mown lawn is strong enough to tempt even the saintliest of environmentalists
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/07.text:
The garden guru has spoken and I can unshackle myself from the bonds of guilt. Actually that’s me and several million like-minded folk. We leapt upon Monty Don’s words over the weekend. “This spring and summer I have made a tightly mown and evenly green lawn,” he said, letting slip a U-turn as monumental as Napoleon’s retreat from Russia in 1812. “This is slightly surprising,” he added, “because I have long been on the record for advocating replacing lawns with long grass, ideally filled with naturalised flowers.”
You don’t say. This mower fanatic, and I am indeed a foot soldier in the legion of lawn lunatics – we must mow and we must mow often – had been cowed in the wake of Don’s previous utterances.
I shan’t forget the fateful blow he dealt us back in March 2021, talking of “the obsession” for mowing, “which tends to be male, which is controlling rather than embracing”. He then went from psychological attack to environmental: “Cutting grass,” he said, “burns lots of fossil fuel, makes a filthy noise and is about the most injurious thing you can do to wildlife.”
We should let the grass grow, he pleaded, and the eco-radicals, who each year bang on about No Mow May, hoisted him to their metaphorical shoulders. As we simple Middle Englanders retreated to our sheds and garages, cast an eye over our beloved machines, our ride-ons, push/hover/fly mowers and our strimmers and shed a gentle tear.
And ever since we’ve had to mow with a heavy burden of shame, embarrassed by the roar of our engines and, dispensing fuel, casting a furtive eye over our shoulder as if we were mid-bank heist.
But now Don has recanted, rediscovering the joy of mowing – not perhaps the peace that we seek, the blissful solace we find, undisturbed from our loved ones, subsumed under the roar of the engine, but the pleasure of lines, of light and shade and of the balance between the mown and the un-mown. That taste of joy, like the first sip of white Burgundy after a period off the wagon.
“Long grass fills a space to quite a surprising extent,” he now says, “whereas mown grass takes the same area and expands it. Gardens need room for the eye and mind to drift and breathe.”
Which is indeed the mower’s defence. We who mow seriously see philosophy in our work, not simply a relentless attack on growth and weeds. The neat lawn becomes a greater entity when it compares with the long grass. And because we have deigned it to be such, we relish our little opportunity to play God. There is always a thrill to allow, say, grass to grow in an orchard, and then to cut a path through it.
So there is sympathy with nature here, while we disparage the fanatics. Of which Don became one. Having led the charge with rants about male control and climate devastation, he now sees the light. And his recantation is a fabulous and simple morality tale. We mow because we just want the place to look nice, to show visitors that we care, that we’re not scruffy, that we want pretty areas to sit out in and for children to run about in.
In a week in which Just Stop Oil disruptors are getting to know His Majesty’s prisons, wouldn’t it be sweet if other eco-fanatics also had a good, head-long collision with reality? I’ll sit outside, feel my toes on the freshly cut grass and sip a glass of rosé to that.
